chunks: Ali ibn Ibrahim, from his father, from Hammad, from Hariz, from Zurara, from Abu Ja'far (peace be upon him), who said:
I said to him, 'What is the ruling on prayer behind a slave?' He said, 'There is no problem with it if he is a jurist (faqih), and there is not anyone more learned than him there.'
I said, 'Can I pray behind the blind man?' He said, 'Yes, if there is someone to guide him (to face the Qiblah), and he is the best of them.'

He said, 'And the Commander of the Faithful (peace be upon him) said: None of you should pray behind the leper, the one with vitiligo, the insane, the physically restricted, the son of adultery, and the Bedouin should not lead the Muhajirun (immigrants).
ai.seo_question: Who is eligible to lead prayer behind according to Shia jurisprudence?
ai.summary: This narration from al-Kafi highlights the Shia juristic principle that spiritual and intellectual merit (fiqh) can supersede social status or physical perfection, as evidenced by the permissibility of a slave or blind person leading prayer if they are the most learned. It complements this with specific exclusions for those with distinct physical or social markers, such as lepers or sons of adultery, while also noting the historical tension between Bedouin and settled Arab communities in early Islamic leadership.
